title: Detection of Business Relationships
summary: This detection strategy looks for adversary collection of information about your business relationships, meaning the suppliers, vendors, partners and contractors that your organisation depends on. An attacker who maps those relationships can send a convincing message that appears to come from a trusted partner, or can aim at a smaller supplier whose access controls are weaker. The telemetry that helps is web server access logs for partner and supplier pages, certificate transparency monitoring for look alike domains, domain registration monitoring and inbound mail gateway records. The strategy fails in practice because most of this collection happens on somebody else's infrastructure, so you usually see only the last step, when a look alike partner domain sends mail to your staff.

beginner.definition: A business relationship is any company that you work with, such as a supplier or a partner. Attackers study these links before they strike. They want to know who you trust, so they can pretend to be that company. This detection looks for signs that somebody is mapping those links or copying a partner name.
beginner.whyItMatters: Most people trust a message from a known supplier. An attacker who learns the name of your supplier can send invoices, files or links that look normal. A smaller supplier often has weaker security than you do, so the attacker may enter your network through them. Your own logs rarely show the research stage of that plan. What you can see is a strange domain asking about your partners. You can also see mail that arrives from a name almost like the real one.
howItWorks: Your web server writes a log line each time somebody requests a page from your public site.
The detection counts requests that touch partner, supplier and vendor pages from one source address.
Separately, a monitoring feed reports new certificates issued for names that resemble your partners.
Your mail gateway extracts the sender domain from every inbound message and compares it to an approved list.
When a look alike partner domain appears in mail, or one web source reads only partner pages, the rule alerts.
beginner.example: Think of a hospital sign in sheet at the reception desk. A visitor writes a name and the person they came to see. A thief can read that sheet and learn which doctor works with which clinic. The thief then buys a white coat and says he is from that clinic. Nothing on the sheet was secret, but the pattern of visits was valuable. Your detection acts like a receptionist who notices the same stranger reading the sheet every morning. The receptionist cannot arrest anyone, but she can write down the time and tell security to watch the door.
takeaways: Attackers study your partners so they can borrow the trust you give them.
A look alike sender domain is often the first clue you can actually see.
Public partner pages are not secret, but the pattern of access still matters.

objectives: Explain why an attacker maps your suppliers and business partners.
Identify the log sources that record collection against partner pages.
Describe how to compare a sender domain with an approved partner list.
Build a query that flags look alike partner names in inbound mail.
Recommend controls that reduce the risk of supplier impersonation.
dataSources: Reverse proxy or web server access logs for partner, supplier and vendor pages, with source address and user agent
Certificate transparency monitoring results for newly issued certificates on names similar to approved partners
Inbound mail gateway logs with sender domain, reply to address and message authentication results
Domain registration and name server change monitoring for typo squatting variants of partner domains
Employee reports forwarded to the phishing mailbox that quote the name of a partner
logic: The pattern is collection against the public information that describes your business relationships, followed by impersonation of one of those partners. The fields to correlate are the source address in web access logs, the set of pages it requests, the sender domain and reply to address in inbound mail, and the approved partner list held by procurement. Benign access to partner pages comes from search engine crawlers, sales teams and journalists, and their request patterns are wide rather than narrow. The malicious case shows narrow interest in partner pages from one source, or mail that uses a partner name with a domain that is not on the approved list.
pseudoQuery:
# title: Inbound Mail From Look-alike Partner Domain
# logsource:
#   product: network
# detection:
#   selection:
#     event_type: 'smtp_message_accepted'
#     sender_domain_matches_partner_name: 'true'
#     sender_domain_on_approved_list: 'false'
#   filter_bulk_mailer:
#     sender_domain|endswith: '.mailer.example'
#   condition: selection and not filter_bulk_mailer
# level: low
falsePositives: A partner that sends mail through a bulk mailing platform with its own sending domain.
A newly onboarded supplier whose domain has not yet been added to the approved list.
Marketing tools that send on behalf of a partner and use a tracked reply to address.
A regional office of a partner that uses a different country domain for local business.
tuningNotes: Build the approved partner domain list with procurement and review it every month, because a missing entry is the main source of false alarms. Add a filter for the bulk mailing platforms that partners legitimately use. Scope the web part of the rule to the pages that list suppliers or partners, and exclude search engine crawler user agents. Whitelisting too aggressively removes the ability to catch a partner that has genuinely been breached, so keep unlisted but similar domains at low severity for analyst review.
